To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the proliferation of immature plasma cell lineage cells in the pouch mucosa of patients who have undergone restorative proctectomy for UC is a significant finding.
the proliferation of immature plasma cell lineages is increased in the inflamed ileal pouch of patients with ulcerative proctocolitis.
immature plasma cells, as indicated by co‐expression of CD19 and CD138, proliferate in inflamed pouch tissue in UC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the etiopathogenesis of pouchitis in patients with ulcerated colitis.
the etiology and pathogenesis of pouch‐itis.
the proliferation of immature plasma cell lineage in UC‐derived pouchitis mucosa.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the increased numbers of immature plasma cells are a specific and significant feature of the pouchitis mucosal lesions in patients with UC, and that the increased number of CD138+ cells is the result of increased proliferation of these immature plasma lineage cells.
there is an increased number of immature plasma cells, which may be the cause of the pouchitis.
there is a significant increase in the number of Ki‐67+CD19+ immature plasma cells and Ki‐67+ CD138+ immature plasma cells, and CD19+CD 138+ cells in pouchitis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the immature B‐cell lineage cells proliferated in the inflamed mucosa and ulcer base of UC, and the immature B‐lymphocyte and plasma lineage cells were increased in the inflamed ileal pouch mucosal of UC.
the immature B cells are involved in pouchitis.

the proliferation of immature plasma cell lineage cells is a specific and significant finding in the inflamed mucosa and ulcer bases of UC and that the increased proliferation of immature plasma‐cell‐lineage cells is a significant finding in the pouchitis of patients with UC, but not in the normal pouch of patients with FAP.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have found a new marker for the diagnosis of pouchitis.
there may be an autoimmune component to the etiology of pouch‐itis, and the abnormality may be derived from UC itself.
the proliferation of immature plasma‐lineage cells in the mucosa of the ileal pouch may contribute to the pathogenesis of UC‐related pouchitis.
